metadata.title: Important Things to Know Before Developing Artificial Intelligence-Based Drone Learning Systems: From the Experience of Educational Practice
metadata.venue: International Journal of Online Pedagogy and Course Design

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a task-based drone learning module implemented in four schools in Taiwan (A–D) with a summer-camp style intervention. The manuscript does not report the use of any complex survey design weights (e.g., sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures, and the analysis is based on pre/post attainment tests and questionnaire/checklist scores. Because the design is an educational practice study with purposive recruitment of learners into school-based settings rather than a probability sample, analysts should not expect ILSA-style population-representative weighting variables to be available. For any re-analysis, the appropriate approach would be to treat the data as a clustered educational setting (students nested in schools) and use school-level clustering/robust inference if supported, but the paper itself does not specify weight variables.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The study does not use plausible values (PVs) because the outcomes are not ILSA-style cognitive achievement PV scores; instead, they use a researcher-developed attainment test (multiple-choice) and questionnaire/checklist scales for motivated strategies and computational thinking. Missing-data handling is not described, which is a reporting gap because the paper reports correlations and regression/ANOVA results but does not state whether any participants/items were excluded due to missing responses or how missing questionnaire/checklist entries were treated.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study recruited 73 learners aged 11–15 from four schools in Taoyuan City, Taiwan (A–D). Learners participated in a drone learning experiment using a task-based module with eight drone tasks (Tasks A–H) implemented over summer-camp style sessions (three days for the initial recruitment in School A; 120 minutes for School B; summer-camp classes for Schools C and D). The manuscript does not specify additional inclusion/exclusion criteria beyond participation in the drone learning activities and completion of the pre/post attainment tests and post-learning questionnaires/checklists.

main_findings.dataset_used: Drone learning module (Taiwan Taoyuan) — pre/post attainment test (11–15 years)
main_findings.target_variable: Drone programming attainment (pre/post attainment test score)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Paired-samples t-test: t = 24.051***; Programming attainment prediction via multiple regression: R² = 0.20 (adjusted R² = 0.17). Significant predictors: problem-solving β = .313, p < .01; creativity β = -.276, p < .05; gender β = .217, p = .05 (not significant as a predictor in the regression).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the drone learning module in Taiwan (Taoyuan) with pre/post attainment test the study leveraged gender, problem-solving, and creativity to predict drone programming attainment, finding that problem-solving positively predicted attainment while creativity showed a negative association and gender did not significantly predict attainment in the regression. This indicates that strengthening collaborative problem-solving supports drone programming learning gains more reliably than relying on creativity alone, informing instructional design and scaffolding priorities for STEAM drone tasks.

data.outcome_summary: This study used a task-based drone learning module in four schools in Taoyuan, Taiwan, with 73 learners aged 11–15. Learners completed an attainment test on drone concepts and Blockly programming before and after the drone tasks, and the paper also administered a motivated strategies questionnaire (MSLQ-based) and a computational thinking checklist. The pre/post attainment scores increased substantially (paired-samples t-test: t = 24.051***), and multiple regression explained a modest share of attainment variance (R² = 0.20; adjusted R² = 0.17), with problem-solving (β = .313, p < .01) and creativity (β = -.276, p < .05) emerging as significant predictors. The study further reports that self-efficacy was lower than other motivated-strategy dimensions, while cooperativity was highest among computational thinking factors. Limitations include the absence of reported missing-data handling and no explicit discussion of how school-level clustering was handled statistically.
